text: Supplied with water. <break time="0.8s" /> Any good marathoner probably has the endurance to chase down a zebra, antelope, or steenbok. <break time="0.8s" /> However there is more to persistence hunting than endurance. <break time="0.8s" /> A lot more. <break time="0.8s" /> Endurance hunters need to be able. <break time="0.8s" /> To recognize specific target prey. <break time="0.8s" /> And then track that specific individual. <break time="0.8s" /> Over long distances. <break time="0.8s" /> Almost any animal we might want to pursue. <break time="0.8s" /> Is much faster than we are in a sprint. <break time="0.8s" /> And will immediately disappear into the distance. <break time="0.8s" /> To exploit our endurance edge. <break time="0.8s" /> We need to be able to track a specific individual. <break time="0.8s" /> For several hours. <break time="0.8s" /> By identifying and reading their spoor. <break time="0.8s" /> And anticipating their actions. <break time="0.8s" /> The ability to distinguish the target, say a zebra, from other zebras. <break time="0.8s" /> Is crucial. <break time="0.8s" /> Since many herd animals have a defensive strategy. <break time="0.8s" /> In which they circle back to their herd. <break time="0.8s" /> And try to disappear. <break time="0.8s" /> By blending back into the group. <break time="0.8s" /> If you cannot selectively target the one you have been chasing. <break time="0.8s" /> The tired one. <break time="0.8s" /> Then you could end up chasing a fresh zebra. <break time="0.8s" /> A disaster. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus persistence hunters must be able. <break time="0.8s" /> To track and identify individuals.
